title: McCloskey & Co. v. Minweld Steel Co.
lead: A steel subcontractor reports procurement trouble and asks for help; the general contractor cancels, but the letter does not amount to an unequivocal anticipatory repudiation.

actors.name: McCloskey & Company
actors.role: General contractor on two state-hospital buildings and plaintiff seeking anticipatory-breach recovery.

actors.name: Minweld Steel Company
actors.role: Steel fabricator and erector under three subcontracts.

actors.name: Travelers
actors.role: Bond provider on two subcontracts and codefendant in one action.

proceedings: The district judge granted defense judgments at the close of McCloskey’s case and denied postjudgment requests.
The Third Circuit affirmed because the plaintiff had not established anticipatory breach.
limits: Pennsylvania law governed these historical contracts. The decision predates any asserted modern statutory adequate-assurance entitlement. It assumes without deciding that McCloskey could set the proposed date and finds no repudiation even on that premise.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Three subcontracts provide steel without a fixed performance date
sections.cue: What duties and default provisions did they contain?
paragraphs: McCloskey & Company, general contractor for two Hollidaysburg State Hospital buildings, engaged Minweld Steel Company to fabricate and erect structural steel and long-span joists. Two agreements were dated May 1, 1950 and a third May 26. Travelers bonded two and later became a codefendant in one of the resulting actions.

Article V allowed material supply or termination on two days’ written notice for specified defaults. Article VI required prompt submissions and delivery at times McCloskey directed so final completion would not be delayed, but the agreements stated no fixed performance date. After receiving drawings in May, Minweld answered a June inquiry with estimates of initial delivery September 1 and completion around November 15.

sources.pinpoint: Subcontracts and delivery estimates;220 F.2d 102–103 & n.1

sections.title: Minweld describes failed supply attempts and requests cooperation
sections.cue: Why could it not give McCloskey’s demanded assurance?
paragraphs: On July 20, McCloskey threatened termination unless Minweld gave unqualified assurance of definite procurement, fabrication and delivery arrangements within thirty days. Minweld’s July 24 response described unsuccessful efforts with Bethlehem, U.S. Steel and Carnegie-Illinois in a tightened market affected by governmental directives.

The letter described completed engineering, an order held for two weeks and then refused, and other producers booked for roughly a year. Minweld could not positively promise supply or dates, but emphasized its wish to avoid delay and complete the undertaking. It asked McCloskey and the project-owning General State Authority to help induce a producer to supply the steel.

sources.pinpoint: July correspondence and full letter;220 F.2d 103–104 & n.2

sections.title: McCloskey cancels and sues after obtaining replacement suppliers
paragraphs: McCloskey treated the letter as an admission of inability to perform and cancelled on July 26. It obtained structural steel from Bethlehem without apparent difficulty, accepted new proposals August 7 and engaged substitute performers. The joists came from Frederick Grundy Iron Works. Bethlehem had originally competed with Minweld.

McCloskey sued for anticipatory breach of each agreement. At the close of its case, the district judge granted defense motions for judgment. McCloskey appealed those results and the July 14, 1954 order denying requests for findings, vacation of judgments and new trials. Federal jurisdiction rested on diversity, and the appellate court applied Pennsylvania law to the apparently Pennsylvania-executed contracts.

sources.pinpoint: Cancellation, replacements and litigation;220 F.2d 102,104–105 & nn.3,6

sections.title: The court separates a desperate supply position from an absolute refusal
sections.cue: Why did uncertainty about preparation not establish breach?
paragraphs: Pennsylvania law required an absolute and unequivocal refusal to perform or a distinct, positive statement of inability. Minweld’s request for help did not abandon every possibility of obtaining steel. A producer might reconsider or another supplier might become available. There was no evidence that earlier attempts necessarily would have succeeded.

The court regarded the letter as realistically confronting difficulty and seeking cooperation that McCloskey should have been willing to provide. McCloskey instead ended the opportunity and obtained replacement materials. The First Restatement also distinguished inadequate preparation before performance was due from a failure to perform when due; threatening eventual performance did not itself establish anticipatory breach.

McCloskey argued that its July 20 demand set a thirty-day delivery date under Article VI. Even assuming that interpretation, Minweld had not repudiated the date; it had failed to provide the requested assurance about preparatory arrangements. These contracts did not authorize that assurance demand. The court therefore could reject the claim without deciding the date-setting issue against McCloskey.

sections.title: The defense judgments survive and the findings objection also fails
sections.cue: What did the appellate court affirm?
paragraphs: The Third Circuit affirmed because McCloskey had not made a prima facie case of anticipatory breach. In note 7 it also held that the trial judge’s memorandum sufficiently supplied findings and conclusions under Rule 52.

Judge McLaughlin wrote for the panel with Judges Goodrich and Hastie, and no separate opinion appeared. The result concerned these contracts and the letter relied on as repudiation; it did not adjudicate a modern statutory right to adequate assurance.

sources.pinpoint: Disposition and procedural note;220 F.2d 105 & n.7
